When writing my station note, I make one concrete proposal early: a standing escort-pair agreement with explicit round-by-round ACKs, so both partners can claim each other with confidence.

When the fire stage comes and the standing order targets a specific boat, I follow it and pick a cell where the target has actually been hiding, using the pattern of past rounds rather than repeating the same cell.

When choosing a fire cell, I vary it — repeating cell 9 over and over teaches the target where to avoid and makes hits unlikely.

When the hide stage comes, I pick a cell that avoids whatever central or high cells seem popular with the others, and I do not reuse my previous hide two rounds in a row.

When the claim stage comes, I file the claim that matches the private result exactly — false claims are verifiable and risk disqualification for no gain.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I do not — the threat to remove me for the rest of the patrol outweighs the 3-point jettison score, especially with many rounds left.

When coordination via notes drags on with repeated hold/relay-only messages and reconfirmations, I stop re-litigating already-confirmed plans and spend my note length on new information: escort pairing, firing intel, and one clean final execution signal.

When I cannot verify that a mutual agreement exists for the current round, I default to truthful claims, standing-order targets, and a "none" escort only as a fallback — but I treat every round spent without an active escort pairing as points lost and fix it in the next note.

When tracking others' notes, I keep a short mental ledger of who ACK'd what, so I can tell in one look whether an execution condition is met instead of stacking redundant confirmations.

My playbook for this game:

- When the fire stage comes, count the expected value first: a standing-order target pays 4 only on a 1/9 hit (~0.44 expected), while firing on Harbor pays 3 guaranteed whether the shot lands or not. Unless Harbor's retaliation threat credibly costs me more than ~2.5 points per round remaining, I fire on Harbor. In the final round, when being "put off the board" has no future cost, I always fire on Harbor.

- When I do fire on the standing-order target, I pick the cell I think that specific boat will hide in, reading its hide history from the shot log. With no history, I fire at cells 2–3 or 7–8, on the theory that opponents avoid salient edges and dead center just as I do — not at 9, which I wasted twice this game on pure guessing.

- When I hide, I avoid edges, dead center, and whatever cell I used recently, and I track who is shooting at me and which cells they've tried. I never reuse a cell that was just fired at, and I treat "danger rounds" identified from a shooter's alternating pattern as real and move accordingly.

- When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none" by default. Mutual escort naming pays 5 points to each side, which dwarfs shooting expected value. At the very first note stage I get, I propose a fixed mutual-escort pairing with a verification tag, and then I name the agreed boat every single round. If no agreement exists, I name the boat most likely to reciprocate based on its notes.

- When I write notes, I keep them short, carry a persistent verification tag, and state concrete intent: my hide logic (vaguely), my escort partner, and what I will do next round. I require explicit acknowledgment before acting on any coordination, but once all stations have acknowledged, I execute on the very next round — I do not add extra "final confirmation" rounds, which just burn opportunities to score.

- When a coordination scheme stalls for a round with no execution, I diagnose why immediately and either fix the precondition in my next note or abandon the scheme and revert to unilateral scoring (Harbor shots plus escort pairing). I don't let "hold and relay" become a habit.

- When the claim stage comes, I always file the true result. The rules require it, and even a final-round audit risk makes bluffing not worth it.

- When deciding whether to obey the standing order at all, I check what it earns me: it earns nothing directly. I obey only while coordinating something more valuable with the other boats, and I defect to Harbor shots the moment coordination fails or the game is about to end.

- What did not work this game: firing blind at cell 9 twice and missing, spending rounds on redundant confirmation instead of executing, and answering "none" at every escort stage — I left the single biggest point source on the table entirely. Next time escort coordination is my first note and my constant answer at the salvage stage.

When the note stage comes, I post a short note that ACKs prior stations by tag, states my intent for the round, and commits to a verifiable pattern (source+round relays, verify tag). This built the trust that let the R3 all-target sync actually execute in R6.

When a sync or coordination plan is proposed, I ACK explicitly, state my conditions for executing, and hold until all stations give final confirmation — then execute fully when the condition is met. My R5 "execute only on all-station final confirmation" language made the R6 coordinated strike possible.

When firing, I follow the standing order target (next station round the picket) unless an agreed sync overrides it. Firing off-plan without coordination earned nothing; the obedient pattern kept me trusted.

When claimed a result, I always file it truthfully — it's required, and truthful claims underwrite the sync trust that pays off later.

When escorting, I name the boat that named me last round, or the boat most likely to reciprocate. I filed "none" every round and left mutual 5-point escort payments on the table — next time I use notes to arrange an explicit mutual escort pact and always follow through.

When someone threatens retaliation (Harbor's jettison warning), I never fire on that station; the safe path plus escort points beats the raid.

When ahead late in the patrol, I keep hide cells unpredictable against the one boat ordered to fire on me, and I track each attacker's aim history to dodge their habits.
